name: Tools & Techniques for IT Project Management
blurb: SPM, process models, requirements, planning, scheduling, quality, HR, risk & docs

questions.q: Software Project Management (SPM) is best described as:
options: A proper way of planning and leading software projects — planning, implementing, monitoring and controlling them
questions.explanation: SPM is a part of project management in which software projects are planned, implemented, monitored and controlled.

questions.q: The 'triple constraints' (basic forces) that drive and define a software project are:
questions.explanation: Unit 1 identifies cost, schedule and quality as the three basic forces at play in industrial-strength software.

questions.q: According to the ISO software product quality standard, which set lists the six quality attributes?
options: Speed, size, cost, colour, weight, shape
Functionality, Reliability, Usability, Efficiency, Maintainability, Portability
Design, Code, Test, Deploy, Review, Audit
Scope, Time, Cost, Quality, Risk, Procurement
questions.explanation: The six software quality attributes are Functionality, Reliability, Usability, Efficiency, Maintainability and Portability.

questions.q: The management myth 'adding more programmers to a late project speeds it up' is false because:
options: Adding manpower to a late project delays it further, as new workers take time to learn the project
More people always triple the output
questions.explanation: Adding more manpower to a project already behind schedule further delays it — new workers take longer to come up to speed (Brooks' Law idea).

questions.q: The three 'R's for improving software maintainability/evolution are:
questions.explanation: Unit 1 describes Reuse, Reengineering and Retooling as the three R's supporting software evolution.

questions.q: In the PMI framework, the five project management process phases are:
options: Initiation, Planning, Execution, Monitoring & Controlling, Closing
questions.explanation: The PMBOK life cycle has five phases: Initiation, Planning, Execution, Monitoring & Controlling and Closing.

questions.q: A project charter is created in which phase, and what does it contain?
options: Initiation phase; project constraints, goals, appointment of the project manager, budget and timeline
questions.explanation: The project charter is an initiation-phase document with constraints, goals, the PM's appointment, budget and expected timeline — but no technical detail.

questions.q: In the Mendelow stakeholder framework, Influence is defined as:
options: The product of Power and Interest (Power × Interest)
questions.explanation: Mendelow defines Power as ability to influence objectives, Interest as how much stakeholders care, and Influence as Power × Interest.

questions.q: In the Salience stakeholder model, a 'Definitive' stakeholder is one who has:
questions.explanation: The Salience model classifies by power, legitimacy and urgency; a Definitive stakeholder (class 7) has all three and is the most important.

questions.q: In the classical Waterfall model, a major drawback is that it:
options: Has no feedback path and is difficult to accommodate change requests
questions.explanation: The classical waterfall model has no feedback path for error correction and cannot easily accommodate changing requirements.

questions.q: The V-Model is also known as the:
questions.explanation: The V-Model associates a testing (validation) phase with each development (verification) stage, giving it its V shape.

questions.q: Which SDLC model combines iterative development with systematic risk analysis, passing through four phases in iterations called spirals?
questions.explanation: The Spiral model combines iterative development with the waterfall's control, placing very high emphasis on risk analysis across four phases.

questions.q: In Extreme Programming (XP), 'pair programming' is part of which practice, and what is TDD?
options: Code Review; Test-Driven Development where test cases are written before code
questions.explanation: XP uses pair programming for code review and Test-Driven Development (TDD), in which test cases are written even before any code is written.

questions.q: The RAD (Rapid Application Development) model is built around which phases?
options: Business Modelling, Data Modelling, Process Modelling, Application Generation, Testing & Turnover
questions.explanation: RAD distributes work into Business Modelling, Data Modelling, Process Modelling, Application Generation and Testing & Turnover, using prototyping and automation tools.

questions.q: The three types of software maintenance described in the waterfall model are:
questions.explanation: Maintenance types are Corrective (fix errors), Perfective (enhance functionality) and Adaptive (port to a new environment).

questions.q: Non-functional requirements differ from functional requirements in that they:
options: Describe what the system should do
Constrain the services/functions (e.g. performance, reliability, security) and often apply to the system as a whole
questions.explanation: Non-functional requirements are constraints on services (timing, reliability, security, etc.) that usually apply to the system as a whole.

questions.q: In a Data Flow Diagram (DFD), which convention uses circles for processes while Gane & Sarson use rounded rectangles?
questions.explanation: Yourdon-Coad and Yourdon-DeMarco use circles for processes; Gane & Sarson use rounded rectangles (lozenges).

questions.q: A context-level DFD that represents the entire system as a single process is also called:
questions.explanation: The context diagram shows the whole system as one process with its external entities and is referred to as the Level 0 DFD.

questions.q: In Function Point Analysis, the Value Adjustment Factor (VAF) is computed as:
questions.explanation: VAF = (TDI × 0.01) + 0.65, where TDI is the Total Degree of Influence (0–70); then FPC = UFP × VAF.

questions.q: In the COCOMO model, which project class suits a small team, stable environment and well-understood problem?
questions.explanation: Organic projects involve small teams with good experience and less-than-rigid requirements (e.g. simple inventory systems).

questions.q: The purpose of a Business Case in the IT project methodology is to:
options: Provide senior management the information needed to decide whether a project should be funded, analysing value/feasibility/costs/benefits/risks of alternatives
questions.explanation: A business case analyses organisational value, feasibility, costs, benefits and risks of alternatives so management can make an informed funding decision.

questions.q: In the non-numeric 'Sacred Cow' project selection model, a project is selected because:
options: A senior/powerful official suggested it, and it continues until finished or the boss ends it
It scored highest in a weighting matrix
It has the shortest payback period
questions.explanation: The Sacred Cow model selects a project simply because a senior, powerful official proposed it; it continues until completed or the boss cancels it.

questions.q: Which numeric project-selection model is also called the Net Present Value (NPV) method?
questions.explanation: The Discounted Cash Flow method is the NPV method — it discounts all cash flows by the required rate of return; a positive sum means the project is acceptable.

questions.q: The Balanced Scorecard approach evaluates a project across which four perspectives?
options: Financial, Customer, Internal Business Processes, Innovation & Learning
questions.explanation: The Balanced Scorecard balances Financial, Customer, Internal Business Processes, and Innovation & Learning perspectives.

questions.q: In scope management, 'Scope creep' refers to:
options: The inability to define the project scope at all
Adding features once the scope has already been approved, lengthening the schedule and causing cost overruns
questions.explanation: Scope creep is adding features after the scope is approved; scope grove is inability to define scope; scope leap changes the MOV.

questions.q: The WBS '8/80 rule' states that a work package should take:
options: No less than 8 hours and no more than 80 hours of effort
questions.explanation: The 8/80 rule suggests a work package should require no less than 8 hours and no more than 80 hours of effort.

questions.q: In risk planning, Risk Exposure (RE) is calculated as:
options: RE = Probability of the risk × Cost (impact)
questions.explanation: Risk Exposure RE = Probability of the risk × Cost (size of loss); it is used to identify top risks and mitigation strategies.

questions.q: The software effort-distribution '40-20-40 rule' allocates effort as:
options: 40% front-end analysis & design, 20% coding, 40% back-end testing
questions.explanation: The 40-20-40 rule allocates 40% to front-end analysis/design, 20% to coding and 40% to back-end testing.

questions.q: The two quantitative scheduling techniques used to identify the chain of dependent tasks determining project duration are:
options: PERT (Program Evaluation and Review Technique) and CPM (Critical Path Method)
questions.explanation: PERT and CPM are quantitative techniques that identify the critical path — the chain of dependent tasks determining project duration.

questions.q: In the Critical Path Method, the critical path is:
options: The shortest path with the most float
The longest-duration path through the network, which has zero float and determines the minimum project duration
Any path chosen by the manager
The path with the fewest activities
questions.explanation: The critical path is the longest path through the network; it has zero float and defines the shortest time to complete the project.

questions.q: The two schedule-compression techniques are:
options: Crashing (adding resources) and Fast-tracking (doing tasks in parallel)
questions.explanation: Crashing applies more resources to the critical path; fast-tracking performs activities in parallel — both compress the schedule.

questions.q: In communication overhead, the total number of communication channels among N people is given by:
questions.explanation: The number of communication channels among N people is C = N(N−1)/2, so overhead grows rapidly as team size increases.

questions.q: A Fixed-Price (firm fixed-price / lump-sum) contract primarily places the risk of cost overruns on:
questions.explanation: Fixed-price contracts define a total price and require the seller to assume the risk of cost overruns.

questions.q: Which cost-reimbursable contract type is described as 'the pits for the buyer' because the vendor can run up costs by wasting materials?
questions.explanation: Cost plus percentage of costs is worst for the buyer — the vendor can waste materials and still be paid a percentage on the replacements.

questions.q: When only one qualified seller exists in the marketplace, the procurement situation is called:
questions.explanation: Sole source = only one qualified seller exists; single source = the org prefers a specific seller; oligopoly = very few sellers.

questions.q: Which document is a request FROM a buyer TO sellers asking them to provide a solution (not just a price)?
questions.explanation: An RFP requests sellers to provide a proposal/solution; an RFQ/IFB requests a price, and bids/quotes come from sellers with price as the deciding factor.

questions.q: In the SEI Capability Maturity Model (CMM), the five levels in order are:
questions.explanation: CMM levels are Level 1 Initial, Level 2 Repeatable, Level 3 Defined, Level 4 Managed and Level 5 Optimizing.

questions.q: McCall's software quality model groups 11 factors into which three categories?
options: Product Operation, Product Revision, Product Transition
questions.explanation: McCall groups the 11 quality factors into Product Operation, Product Revision and Product Transition categories.

questions.q: Six Sigma's structured improvement methodology for existing processes is known by the acronym:
questions.explanation: Six Sigma uses DMAIC (Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve, Control) and DMADV for new designs.

questions.q: Philip Crosby's 'Zero Defects' concept, as adopted by Six Sigma, is quantified as:
options: 3.4 defects per million opportunities (DPMO), allowing a 1.5-sigma shift
questions.explanation: Under the Six Sigma standard, 'zero defects' is defined as 3.4 defects per million opportunities (allowing a 1.5-sigma process shift).

questions.q: Ishikawa's cause-and-effect diagram is also commonly called a:
questions.explanation: The Ishikawa (cause-and-effect) diagram is called a fishbone diagram because the effect is the 'head' and causes form the 'bones'.

questions.q: In a control chart, the 'Rule of Seven' indicates an out-of-control process when:
options: Seven data points in a row fall above or below the mean
questions.explanation: The Rule of Seven (Seven Run Rule) flags seven consecutive points on one side of the mean as a non-random, out-of-control signal.

questions.q: Software reliability is measured by Mean Time Between Failures, calculated as:
questions.explanation: MTBF = MTTF (Mean Time To Failure) + MTTR (Mean Time To Repair); availability = (MTTF/MTBF) × 100.

questions.q: In Maslow's hierarchy of needs, which need is the single 'growth need' at the top (the rest being deficiency needs)?
questions.explanation: The bottom four (physiological, safety, social, esteem) are deficiency needs; self-actualization at the top is the growth need.

questions.q: The five main types of power a project manager can use include coercive, legitimate, reward, referent and:
questions.explanation: The five main power types are coercive, legitimate, expert, reward and referent power.

questions.q: A responsibility assignment matrix that maps work from the OBS to responsible and performing units is abbreviated:
questions.explanation: A RAM (Responsibility Assignment Matrix) allocates work to responsible (R) and performing (P) organizations/teams/individuals.

questions.q: The Myers-Briggs Type Indicator (MBTI) measures personality across how many dimensions, including Judgment/Perception?
questions.explanation: MBTI has four dimensions: Extrovert/Introvert, Sensation/Intuition, Thinking/Feeling and Judgment/Perception.

questions.q: Lewin's model of organisational change consists of which three stages?
questions.explanation: Lewin's change model has three stages: Unfreezing the status quo, Changing (the neutral zone), and Refreezing the new state.

questions.q: The five conflict-handling approaches described are avoidance, accommodation, forcing, compromise and:
questions.explanation: The five approaches are avoidance, accommodation (smoothing), forcing, compromise, and collaboration (best when risks/benefits are high).

questions.q: McGregor's Theory X assumes that:
options: People are self-motivated and seek responsibility
People are indolent, resist work, and must be persuaded, rewarded and punished by management
questions.explanation: Theory X assumes people resist work and must be controlled; Theory Y assumes motivation and growth potential are latent in most people.

questions.q: In Herzberg's theory, factors such as achievement, recognition and growth opportunity are called:
questions.explanation: Herzberg calls achievement, recognition, the work itself and growth 'motivators'; physical conditions and peer relations are 'hygiene factors'.

questions.q: In the default modern project organisation, which four teams are defined?
options: Software Management, Software Architecture, Software Development, Software Assessment
questions.explanation: The default organisation has the Software Management, Software Architecture, Software Development and Software Assessment teams.

questions.q: In process automation, the automation support at the project (macroprocess) level is called a(n):
questions.explanation: Metaprocess (line of business) support is an infrastructure; macroprocess (project) support is an environment; microprocess support is a tool.

questions.q: The quality-indicator metric MTBF and Maturity classifies a non-deterministic fault (coincidental with a probabilistic situation, e.g. a design error) as a:
questions.explanation: Deterministic errors are Bohr-bugs (e.g. coding errors); non-deterministic, probabilistic errors are Heisen-bugs (e.g. design errors).

questions.q: In risk assessment, the priority of a risk is computed as p = r × s, where r and s are:
options: The probability of the risk coming true (r) and the severity of loss (s)
questions.explanation: Risk priority p = r × s, where r is the probability of the risk occurring and s is the severity of the resulting loss.

questions.q: The three main strategies to plan for a risk are to avoid it, reduce it, or:
options: Transfer it (e.g. to a third party or via insurance)
questions.explanation: Risk can be avoided, transferred (to a third party / insurance) or reduced; Risk Leverage compares the reduction in exposure to the cost of reduction.

questions.q: The Delphi technique for risk identification works by:
options: A panel of independent experts answering questionnaires over multiple anonymous rounds until they converge
questions.explanation: The Delphi method pools independent experts through multiple anonymous questionnaire rounds, converging toward consensus while removing hierarchy/personality influence.

questions.q: In PERT, the expected (weighted average) time for an activity is calculated as:
questions.explanation: PERT expected time = (optimistic SP + 4 × most-likely MT + pessimistic LT) / 6, which allows for uncertainty.

questions.q: The three main functions of contracts in risk allocation are work transfer, risk transfer and:
options: Motive transfer (implanting motives in the contractor matching the client's)
questions.explanation: Contracts perform work transfer, risk transfer, and motive transfer — implanting motives in the contractor that match the client's.

questions.q: In a RACI chart, how many people should be 'Accountable' for each task?
options: Exactly one (only one accountable person, no more)
questions.explanation: In RACI (Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed), every task should have exactly one Accountable person and no more.

questions.q: In the version-control numbering convention described, the first final/approved version of a document is numbered:
questions.explanation: Drafts are numbered 0-1, 0-2, 0-3…; the first final/approved version is 1-0, and later revisions become 1-1, 1-2… up to 2-0.

questions.q: Document control encompasses six functions: creation, review, modification, certification, issuance and:
questions.explanation: Document control covers Creation, Review, Modification, Certification, Issuance and Distribution.

questions.q: Reviews held at the end of each project phase to decide whether to proceed to the next phase are called:
questions.explanation: Phase-gate reviews (stage-gates / kill-points) occur at the end of each phase to review performance and decide whether to proceed.

questions.q: The lessons-learned process consists of which five steps?
questions.explanation: The lessons-learned process has five steps: Identify, Document, Analyze, Store and Retrieve (with keyword search for retrieval).

questions.q: A lessons-learned session should ideally be facilitated by:
options: Someone other than the project manager, to ensure all relevant items are included
questions.explanation: To get optimum results the session should be facilitated by someone other than the PM, and should ask: what went right, what went wrong, what needs improvement.
